Job 1: Job lives "in the land of Uz" (Job 1:1), probably east of Israel near Edom (Lamentations 4:21). As head of his family, he offers sacrifices himself, as the patriarchs did; the book names no king, law, or temple.
Job 2: In the land of Uz, on another day when the sons of God come before the LORD (Job 2:1). The friends travel from their own homes: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite (Job 2:11).
Job 3: In the land of Uz, after the seven days and seven nights of silence (Job 2:13).
Job 4: The first round of speeches begins with Eliphaz the Temanite.
Job 5: Eliphaz continues the first round of speeches.
Job 6: Job answers Eliphaz in the first round.
Job 7: Job continues his first answer, now speaking to God.
Job 8: Bildad the Shuhite speaks in the first round.
Job 9: Job answers Bildad in the first round.
Job 10: Job continues his answer to Bildad, addressing God.
Job 11: The end of the first round of speeches. Zophar speaks after Eliphaz and Bildad have had their turn (Job 4:1; 8:1; 11:1).
Job 12: Job answers Zophar in the longest reply of the first round (Job 12–14).
Job 13: Job continues answering Zophar and asks to argue his case with God.
Job 14: Job's answer to Zophar ends the first round of speeches.
Job 15: Eliphaz opens the second round of speeches.
Job 16: Job answers Eliphaz in the second round.
Job 17: Job continues his answer to Eliphaz: "My days are past" (Job 17:11).
Job 18: Bildad speaks in the second round.
Job 19: Job answers Bildad in the second round, including "I know that my redeemer liveth" (Job 19:25).
Job 20: Zophar speaks for the last time, closing the second round.
Job 21: Job answers Zophar, ending the second round.
Job 22: Eliphaz opens the third round of speeches.
Job 23: Job answers Eliphaz in the third round.
Job 24: Job continues his answer to Eliphaz, describing the poor driven off the land by those who move landmarks (Job 24:2–4).
Job 25: The third round of speeches, which ends early: Bildad's speech is short, and Zophar does not speak again (Job 25:1; 27:1).
Job 26: Job answers Bildad, beginning his closing speeches (Job 26–31).
Job 28: A poem on where wisdom is found describes ancient mining for silver, gold, iron, and copper (Job 28:1–2).
Job 29: Job recalls his former life, when he sat at the city gate among the elders.
Job 31: Job swears his innocence. "The words of Job are ended" (Job 31:40).
Job 32: Elihu, a younger man, "the son of Barachel the Buzite" (Job 32:2), begins to speak. Buz was a son of Abraham's brother Nahor (Genesis 22:21).
Job 33: Elihu continues his first speech, addressed to Job.
Job 34: Elihu's second speech is addressed to the wise men present.
Job 35: Elihu's third speech is addressed to Job.
Job 37: Elihu's final speech ends with a storm gathering.
Job 38: In the land of Uz, after Elihu's last words, as a storm gathers (Job 37:1–5).
Job 39: God's first speech continues with the wild animals: goats, the ass, the ostrich, the horse, the hawk.
Job 40: Job replies briefly, and God's second speech begins with behemoth.
Job 41: God's second speech ends with leviathan.
Job 42: Job replies, and the book returns to prose. Job lives another 140 years (Job 42:16).
Proverbs 1: "The proverbs of Solomon the son of David, king of Israel" (Proverbs 1:1). Solomon is said to have spoken three thousand proverbs (1 Kings 4:32). Chapters 1–9 are a father's instruction to his son.
Proverbs 3: The father's instruction continues (Proverbs 1–9), including honoring God with the firstfruits.
Proverbs 4: The father's instruction continues, recalling his own father's teaching (Proverbs 4:3–4).
Proverbs 5: The father's instruction continues with a warning against the strange woman.
Proverbs 6: The father's instruction continues with warnings about surety, laziness, and adultery.
Proverbs 7: A father describes watching from his window as a young man is led astray (Proverbs 7:6–7).
Proverbs 8: Wisdom speaks as a woman calling at the city gates.
Proverbs 9: The first collection ends with Wisdom and Folly each inviting the simple to a meal.
Proverbs 10: A new heading, "The proverbs of Solomon" (Proverbs 10:1), begins the main collection of short sayings (Proverbs 10:1–22:16).
Proverbs 12: Solomon's short sayings continue, many contrasting the righteous and the wicked.
Proverbs 13: Solomon's short sayings continue, including "Hope deferred maketh the heart sick" (Proverbs 13:12).
Proverbs 14: Solomon's short sayings continue, including sayings on a king and his people (Proverbs 14:28, 35).
Proverbs 15: Solomon's short sayings continue, from here more often in parallel than in contrast.
Proverbs 16: Solomon's short sayings continue, with several about kings.
Proverbs 17: Solomon's short sayings continue, including "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine" (Proverbs 17:22).
Proverbs 18: Solomon's short sayings continue, including "The name of the LORD is a strong tower" (Proverbs 18:10).
Proverbs 19: Solomon's short sayings continue, with several about the poor (Proverbs 19:1, 4, 7, 17).
Proverbs 20: Solomon's short sayings continue, beginning "Wine is a mocker" (Proverbs 20:1).
Proverbs 21: Solomon's short sayings continue, beginning "The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD" (Proverbs 21:1).
Proverbs 22: The Solomon collection ends at Proverbs 22:16; "the words of the wise" begin at verse 17. Proverbs 22:17–24:22 closely resembles the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope.
Proverbs 24: A second short collection begins: "These things also belong to the wise" (Proverbs 24:23).
Proverbs 25: "These are also proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out" (Proverbs 25:1), about 700 BC.
Proverbs 26: The Hezekiah collection continues with sayings on fools, sluggards, and gossips.
Proverbs 27: The Hezekiah collection continues, including sayings on flocks and herds (Proverbs 27:23–27).
Proverbs 30: "The words of Agur the son of Jakeh" (Proverbs 30:1). Agur is not mentioned anywhere else; "the prophecy" may also be read as a place name, Massa.
Proverbs 31: "The words of king Lemuel, the prophecy that his mother taught him" (Proverbs 31:1). Lemuel is not known from elsewhere. Verses 10–31 form an alphabetical acrostic in Hebrew.
Ecclesiastes 1: The book opens as the words of "the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem" (Ecclesiastes 1:1); tradition identifies him as Solomon, reflecting late in his reign.
Ecclesiastes 2: The Preacher describes building houses, planting vineyards, and gathering silver, gold, singers, and servants, as a king of Jerusalem could (Ecclesiastes 2:4–9).
Ecclesiastes 3: The Preacher reflects on "a time to every purpose under the heaven" (Ecclesiastes 3:1).
Ecclesiastes 4: The Preacher looks at oppression, labor, and the poor wise youth who becomes king.
Ecclesiastes 5: The Preacher speaks of vows in "the house of God" (Ecclesiastes 5:1) and of officials over officials in the land.
Ecclesiastes 6: The Preacher turns to a specific case: wealth, long life, and children given to someone who still cannot enjoy any of it.
Ecclesiastes 7: A section of proverbs begins: "A good name is better than precious ointment" (Ecclesiastes 7:1).
Ecclesiastes 8: Ecclesiastes 8 turns to counsel about living safely under a king's absolute authority, before returning to the problem of justice delayed.
Ecclesiastes 9: The Preacher tells of a little city besieged by a great king and saved by a poor wise man.
Ecclesiastes 10: The sayings continue in the same short, two-line proverb style, with no new heading, date, or named ruler.
Ecclesiastes 11: The Preacher advises casting bread upon the waters and sowing in the morning and evening.
Ecclesiastes 12: A closing voice describes how the Preacher "taught the people knowledge" and arranged his sayings with care (Ecclesiastes 12:9–10), framing the book's final poem on aging and death.
Song of Solomon 1: "The song of songs, which is Solomon's" (Song of Solomon 1:1). Solomon is said to have written 1,005 songs (1 Kings 4:32). The poem names the tents of Kedar and the vineyards of Engedi.
Song of Solomon 2: The poem names the rose of Sharon, the coastal plain, and a spring setting when "the time of the singing of birds is come" (Song of Solomon 2:12).
Song of Solomon 3: Solomon's wedding procession comes up from the wilderness, guarded by sixty valiant men (Song of Solomon 3:7).
Song of Solomon 4: The poem names Gilead, Lebanon, and mountain peaks of Amana, Shenir, and Hermon.
Song of Solomon 5: The woman searches the city at night and is found by the watchmen.
Song of Solomon 6: The woman is compared to Tirzah, a royal city of the northern kingdom before Samaria (1 Kings 16:23–24), and to Jerusalem.
Song of Solomon 7: The poem names the fishpools of Heshbon, the tower of Lebanon facing Damascus, and Carmel.
Song of Solomon 8: "Solomon had a vineyard at Baalhamon" (Song of Solomon 8:11), let out to keepers.
